sources.title: Human History Map, historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Exact repository entry: xinjiang, label Xinjiang, circa 1914 to 1960. This is an imported map identity, not proof of one continuous sovereign government.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1900 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded predecessor snapshot: target cities fall inside qing-dynasty. The label is an atlas simplification and the Qing itself fell in 1911.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1914 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one Polygon, one ring, 197 positions, bbox about 73.6765 to 96.3388 east and 34.2001 to 49.2326 north.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1930 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature for 1930 to 1938. Its coordinate JSON equals the 1920 target geometry and contains all eight audited regional city points.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1945 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature for 1945 to 1960. The outline remains a single 197-position Polygon while political authority inside it was divided and then transformed.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1960 historical basemap topology
sources.note: At the 1960 seam, target cities move to the broad china atlas id. Xinjiang did not disappear; the map library changed identifiers.

sources.title: Justin M. Jacobs, Empire Besieged: The Preservation of Chinese Rule in Xinjiang, 1884 to 1971
sources.note: UC dissertation abstract and full text: provincial status, post-1911 weak central control, a small Han ruling class, foreign pressure, 1949 incorporation and continuity of Chinese sovereignty as an analytical question.

sources.title: Imperial Repertoires in Republican Xinjiang
sources.note: Open-access University of Washington Press chapter: Qing-trained officials, Yang Zengxin, indirect administration, differentiated rule and Xinjiang’s distance from Beijing during the early Republic.

sources.title: Collapse of Empires and the Nationalist Threat
sources.note: Open-access chapter: cross-border revolution, Soviet influence, local national movements, Yang’s political balancing and the transition after his 1928 assassination.

sources.title: Rise of the Ethnopopulists
sources.note: Open-access chapter: Jin Shuren, rebellion, Sheng Shicai, nationality policy, Soviet intervention, political coalitions and coercion in the 1930s.

sources.title: Raising the Stakes in Nationalist Xinjiang
sources.note: Open-access chapter: Sheng’s purges and geopolitical pivot, Nationalist re-entry, competing programs for local representation and the Ili crisis.

sources.title: The Birth Pangs of Chinese Affirmative Action
sources.note: Open-access University of Washington Press chapter: 1949 transition, 1955 autonomous-region structure, nationality-linked subdivisions and the Production and Construction Corps.

sources.title: Xinjiang and the Modern Chinese State, conclusion
sources.note: Open-access University of Washington Press conclusion: continuity and transformation across imperial, Republican and Communist frontier administration, including the limits of treating political seams as social endings.

sources.title: Uyghur Nation, chapter 3: Imperial and Islamic Reform between Turkistan and Turkey
sources.note: Open-access Harvard University Press chapter: Muslim reform networks, cross-border commerce, Jadid schooling and intellectual connections joining Xinjiang to Russian and Ottoman worlds.

sources.title: Uyghur Nation, chapter 8: The Battle for Xinjiang and the Uyghur Nation
sources.note: Open-access chapter: Yang’s autonomy from Nanjing, political movements in the 1920s and 1930s, conflict and the expanding use of Uyghur as a national name.

sources.title: Wang Ke, The East Turkestan Independence Movement, sample chapter
sources.note: Chinese University of Hong Kong Press sample: 1933 to 34 movement, terminology, the Istqlāl newspaper, political factions and first-hand Chinese and Uyghur evidence with explicit debates over names.

sources.title: U.S. Consul at Tihwa report on the Ining uprising, 10 December 1944
sources.note: Primary diplomatic report: uprising began 7 November, multiethnic participants, fighting around Ining and the consul’s cautious distinction between observed events, Chinese allegations and inference about Soviet help.

sources.title: U.S. Consulate analysis of the Ili situation, 1947
sources.note: Primary diplomatic analysis: Ili conflict, Soviet material and advice, Chinese administration and the author’s admitted dependence on partly unverified or partisan reports.

sources.title: U.S. Consulate report from Tihwa, June 1949
sources.note: Primary report: trade negotiations, Nationalist preparations, roads and supply stations, strained relations with Ili representatives and uncertainty before the Communist takeover.

sources.title: Mao Zedong, Telegram to Xinjiang Political and Military Authorities, 28 September 1949
sources.note: Contemporary political text calling for order, unity and cooperation with the entering PLA. Used as evidence of official language, not as a neutral description of events.

sources.title: Eurasian exchanges: pastoralists, markets and cross-border trade in the early twentieth century
sources.note: Journal of Global History article: tea, furs, scarves, Kashgar rugs and machinery at regional fairs; routes through Khorgos linked Ili, Kashgar, Aksu and Ghulja to wider markets.

sources.title: Nationalism or Geopolitics: The Expansion of the Ili Rebellion, 1944 to 46
sources.note: Social Science History article: state purchase monopolies, sheep, furs, wool and livestock extraction, the 1942 trade crisis and pressures on nomadic communities that fed revolt.

sources.title: Karez water heritage and Republican-era repair in Xinjiang
sources.note: Xinjiang University history PDF: early Republican water reports, Yang Zengxin’s repair proposal, Turpan maintenance, 1,084 working karez in 1949 and 1,237 in 1957.

sources.title: Gunnar Jarring, Return to Kashgar: Central Asian Memoirs in the Present
sources.note: Memoir of 1929 to 30 fieldwork: covered craft bazaars, bargaining, food stalls, pilaf, grilled meat, clothing and carpets. Valuable eyewitness detail, explicitly filtered through a foreign visitor’s memory.

sources.title: Aysima Mirsultan, Divorce settlement among the Uyghurs during the Republican era in Xinjiang
sources.note: Central Asian Survey article based on Khotan and Kashgar legal texts: Islamic-law divorce disputes, child custody, inheritance, village elders, fathers-in-law and women’s positions within varied households.

sources.title: University of Hamburg CSMC, a Kashgar waqf document and everyday life
sources.note: Manuscript research note: a Chaghatay pious-endowment scroll, record forms and the archive’s limits for studying charitable, religious and economic life around Kashgar.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Meshrep
sources.note: Modern safeguarding description of Uyghur meshrep as music, dance, drama, oral literature, foods and games, plus moral mediation and informal learning. Used as continuity evidence, not a 1930 census.

sources.title: The Gunnar Jarring Central Eurasia Collection, Prints from the Swedish Mission in Kashgar
sources.note: Catalog of 1892 to 1938 Eastern Turki publications: 1912 press, primers, geography, science, spelling, silk cultivation and history texts, hospitals, schools and explicit mission provenance.

sources.title: The Gunnar Jarring Collection, 1933 Istïqlāl periodical record
sources.note: Catalog and digitized 74-page Kashgar publication: Eastern Turki language, Istïqlāl title, 1933 date, Mission Press publisher and periodical description and slogan.

sources.title: Print and Power in the Communist Borderlands: The Rise of Uyghur National Culture
sources.note: Harvard dissertation: southern Xinjiang print culture, single-text teaching, conflicts between secular and religious subjects, provincial publishing and post-1949 language institutions.

sources.title: Access to formal education in Xinjiang, 1949 to 1987
sources.note: UCL doctoral thesis: early PRC expansion, higher education, declared equality, unequal access, unified curriculum, language reform and political education across ethnic groups.

sources.title: Farewell, My Uyghur Language: script changes and linguistic memory
sources.note: Modern Asian Studies historical discussion: Arabic-derived writing before the mid-1950s, Cyrillic in the later 1950s and Latin-script reforms around the 1960 seam, with discontinuity for readers.

sources.title: A note on Eastern Turki medical manuscripts in the Gunnar Jarring Collection
sources.note: Uppsala scholarly study of medical manuscripts collected in 1929 to 30 and from missionaries: Eastern Turki remedies, humoral learning and the partial archive of local medical knowledge.

sources.title: Mission and Revolution in Eastern Turkestan, part 2
sources.note: Mission history using institutional records and memoirs: Kashgar hospital, dentistry, doctors and nurses. Useful for facilities and personnel, but written from a missionary perspective.

sources.title: Everyday Life and Sanitary Culture of Xinjiang as Perceived by Soviet Medical Professionals, 1920 to 1940
sources.note: CC BY Quaestio Rossica article, DOI 10.15826/qr.2026.1.1046: Soviet medical reports, epidemic work, adaptation across communities and doctors’ political and cultural biases.

sources.title: People’s China, 1952 report on medical teams in minority areas
sources.note: Contemporary PRC state magazine reporting free-treatment teams, hygiene instruction and maternity and child care in minority regions. Used as an official claim, not independent outcome evidence.

sources.title: TIME, High Wind in Tihwa, 3 July 1944
sources.note: Contemporary publicity account of Henry Wallace’s visit and Governor Sheng displaying what was called the province’s only flush toilet. The boast is treated as anecdote, not census.

sources.title: Refugees, Conscripts, and Constructors: Developmental Narratives and Subaltern Han in Xinjiang
sources.note: Modern China article: early PRC settlement, recruitment of young women, the 1954 construction unit and discrepancies between state development narratives and migrant experiences.

sources.title: Racial Capitalism in an Ethnic Minority Border Region: Husbandry Development in Altay
sources.note: China and Asia article: 1952 to 59 pastoral cooperatives and partnerships, state extraction, mobile Kazakh livelihood and the uneven approach to pastoral collectivization.

sources.title: Changing Agro-Pastoral Livelihoods under Collective and Private Land Use in Xinjiang
sources.note: Peer-reviewed historical overview and Nileke case study: land reform, 1953 to 57 cooperation, 1958 communes and consequences for household and pastoral organization.

sources.title: Muslim, Modern, Model Subjects: Writing Uyghur Women into the Chinese Nation, 1949 to 1966
sources.note: Open-access gender history: official portrayals, women performers, labor and education in the early PRC, and the gap between state model images and individual lives.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Xinjiang from 1914 to 1960 saw warlord rule, revolts, Soviet and Nationalist competition, Communist incorporation, new schools and print, changing family and working life, public-health experiments and enduring oasis and pastoral knowledge.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact target xinjiang is indexed circa 1914 to 1960 and is missing before integration.
Every exact snapshot from 1914 through 1945 is one Polygon with one ring and 197 positions; geometry is stable apart from tiny TopoJSON transform differences.
Ürümqi, Kashgar, Hotan, Turpan, Yining, Altay, Hami and Aksu test inside every target snapshot.
The 1900 predecessor assigns those places to qing-dynasty; the 1960 successor assigns them to china.
The atlas id spans several governing regimes and rival administrations, so the card treats the outline only as a locator.
The 1960 endpoint is a map-library id handoff, not a historical end of Xinjiang or its communities.
No appliesTo linkage is used because the exact id has one indexed record and its card must preserve its own identity caveats.
